1:
That only John reports the raising is accounted for first. Barnes and Clarke give the same answer: the earlier three wrote while Lazarus still lived, and naming him would have exposed him, the priests having taken counsel to put him to death also. Clarke credits the conjecture to Grotius and notes the wide gap here, the dedication in December and this miracle near the following passover; Barnes reckons the interval about four months, John writing for readers outside Palestine who needed it at length. Past that Clarke declines to be drawn: in such matters men may innocently guess, but should assert nothing. Calvin looks at the placing instead: nearly the last act of a life whose end was at hand. Others he had raised, but here he displays his power on a rotting corpse, setting before our eyes a lively image of our own resurrection.

The names draw the philologists. Robertson takes Lazarus as a shortened Eleazar, elsewhere only in Luke's parable and unconnected to that beggar; Lightfoot confirms the shortening from the Jerusalem dialect, which clips the opening aleph, and turns to Martha, common in the Talmud — a Martha daughter of Boethus, rich enough to have tapestry laid from her door to the Temple, later seen dragged by the hair behind Arabian horses, the tender and delicate woman of Deuteronomy 28. Bede reads the name itself: Lazarus signifies helped, and of all whom the Lord raised he was helped most, having lain dead four days. Augustine of Hippo would have us rejoice rather than wonder, it being a greater deed to create men than to raise them.

Mary is identified by an anointing John has not yet narrated, and that divides them. Lightfoot and Clarke want the aorist given full force — she had anointed him formerly, which explains the family's confidence — while Robertson and Ellicott read it as looking ahead to the twelfth chapter. All resist merging the three women: Chrysostom insists she was not the harlot of Luke but grave and earnest, Calvin calls the confusion ignorance, and Robertson, against Bernard, calls the linkage grotesque and cruel to the memory of both Mary of Bethany and Mary Magdalene.

On the message the note is restraint. Augustine hears what the sisters did not say: not come and heal, not speak the word there and it shall be done here, but only, he whom thou lovest is sick — enough that he should know, since he is not one to love and then desert. Chrysostom explains why they sent rather than came: partly confidence, partly that grief kept them at home; Theophylact adds it did not become women to leave the house. Henry catches the pronoun: not he who loveth thee, but he whom thou lovest, our encouragements in prayer being fetched from God himself. Robertson observes that both Greek words for love are used of Christ toward Lazarus here, so the usual distinction cannot be pressed.

The reply is read against the outcome. Barnes and Wesley take not unto death to mean not permanent death, Jesus plainly not denying that Lazarus would die; Robertson sets it beside the sin unto death of the first epistle. Clarke thinks the words went back by the messenger, explaining the sisters' later confidence. Ellicott alone turns the clause forward: the illness would not issue in death, but would be the immediate cause of the death of the Son of Man — Robertson agreeing that raising Lazarus brings Jesus face to face with his own end. Calvin guards for the glory of God from proving too much, God being glorified in the ruin of the reprobate as well; Christ speaks of what belongs to his office, which is to save. John Chrysostom draws the pastoral edge: many are offended when those dear to God fall sick or poor, not knowing it belongs to such above all to endure them.
5:
The Evangelist's word for love is not the sisters' word, and Ellicott makes the difference one of speakers rather than objects: in the mouths of women moved by a brother's illness the word of fullest emotion is natural; in the Evangelist's, the word of chosen friendship. Robertson hears continued love in the imperfect, this being the house where Jesus was so often at home. Gill separates two things the word carries: the everlasting love with which Christ loves all his people alike, and a human affection peculiar to this family, who entertained him generously.

Then the delay, which all feel as a difficulty. Ellicott refuses the two usual solutions — that Christ was testing a faith their message had already shown, or was unwilling to leave the work in hand, which assumes his presence was needed at Bethany — preferring the principle that every hour had its work and every work its hour. Calvin draws the pastoral lesson instead: we are not to judge the love of God from the condition before our eyes, for when we have prayed he often delays, to increase our ardour or exercise our patience; believers must learn to suspend their desires. Clarke puts it as a rule — Christ never denies a lesser favour but to confer a greater. Alcuin and Chrysostom give the plain reason: time was allowed for death and burial, that none might call it a trance. Barnes does the arithmetic, Bethabara lying about a day's journey off, so that a day for the message, two days abiding and a day's travel bring him to a man four days dead.

The proposal to return alarms the disciples. Augustine notes where he was going: the place he had just escaped being stoned. He left as man, in weakness, but returns in power. Robertson calls it suicidal madness by any ordinary reckoning. Clarke and Barnes fix the interval behind their protest, the stoning at the feast of dedication. Calvin will not let their concern pass as pure: each was alarmed for himself, the danger being common, and they allege what is more plausible, anxiety for their Master — as men who dread the cross still seek excuses to hide their indolence.

The answer counts the hours. Gill and Wesley report the reckoning: twelve parts between sunrise and sunset, the same in number all year though much shorter in winter. Clarke turns it into speech for Christ: I have not travelled these twelve hours yet, my last hour is not come, and their malice cannot bring it a moment sooner than God has purposed; I am immortal till my work is done. Robertson insists this is not blind fatalism but the opposite of cowardice, full confidence in the Father's purpose. Ellicott hears the same: the night they dreaded could not come before its appointed time, the day of his life being marked out by limits no less sure. Augustine allegorises: Christ showed himself to be the day by appointing twelve, the hours lightened by the day so that through their preaching the world might believe.

The second half turns inward. Ellicott marks the shift: no light in him is no longer the light of this world but the light within a man. Robertson adds from Westcott that man has the capacity for light but is not its source, noting that ancient pedestrians fastened little lamps to their feet. Calvin makes the calling of God the daylight: whoever undertakes nothing but by God's command has him to guide the road, and may go boldly though a thousand obstructions are interposed, while whoever follows his own suggestions gropes blind. Henry compresses it: light in us is to moral actions what light about us is to natural. Theophylact alone reads it historically, some taking the day for the time before the Passion and the night for the Passion itself, when they would be beset with darkness.
11:
Chrysostom hears a second consolation: they go not to Jerusalem to dispute but to Bethany to wake a friend, and the word our binds them to the errand — Ellicott adding that it reminds them Lazarus was their host too. Augustine refuses to treat the term as euphemism: he was really sleeping — to the Lord asleep, to men who could not raise him dead — and the Lord woke him from the grave as easily as you wake a sleeper from his bed. Robertson notes the perfect of the verb that gave us cemetery.

Why death should be called sleep divides them. Barnes takes the word as tender by design, removing what is dreadful and holding out a resurrection; Clarke thinks the Hebrews used it to signify their belief in immortality; Ellicott observes that poets from Homer down made sleep and death twin sisters. Calvin dissents sharply. Augustine and many since allege the word is used because raising the dead is as easy to God as waking a sleeper is to us, but nothing of the sort was in Christ's mind: profane writers use it as freely, and the plain reason is that a corpse lies without feeling like a man in deep sleep. Wesley keeps it simpler: such is the death of good men in the language of heaven, and the slowness of our understanding makes Scripture descend to our barbarous speech. Henry turns the figure to comfort: a Christian dying does but sleep, and death is better than sleep, being the end of earthly cares rather than a pause in them.

The disciples take the word at the surface, and reasonably: sleep in sickness was a recognised good sign, Barnes and Ellicott note, one of six the Rabbis list. Calvin acquits them of craft: they do not twist his words, they seize gladly on a reason not to go. Chrysostom meets the objection that they must have understood, since none travels two days to wake a sleeper — the Lord's sayings were an enigma to them here as often.

So he says it without the figure. Ellicott notes the plainer words fall short of the deeper truth but are the only ones they can take, and Chrysostom marks what he does not repeat: he says Lazarus is dead, but no longer that he goes to wake him, declining to anticipate his own miracle — a hint against vainglory and empty promises. Gill, Barnes and Clarke explain the gladness alike: had he been present the sisters' entreaties would have prevailed, and the lesser cure would have cost the greater sign. Theophylact says it in a line, that curing the sick is an inferior proof of power. Calvin generalises: the nearer God's works come to the ordinary course of nature the less they are valued, so deliverance had to be delayed until it stood far from any human remedy; when he lets us languish he is promoting our salvation.

Thomas closes the scene. All note that Didymus renders the Hebrew name and both mean twin; Ellicott dismisses the attempts to say whose twin — the sister Lydia of the Apostolical Constitutions, a divided spiritual nature — as elaborate guesses. Whether he proposed to die with Lazarus or with Christ divides Barnes and Calvin, who observes that on the first reading the words are ironical. Clarke reports that some hear peevishness — must we also go? — and answers with a rule: where a saying touches a man's character and will bear both senses, take the favourable one, though most men feed like flies, passing over the whole man to light on his sores. Robertson calls it pessimistic courage. Bede sees an appearance of firmness in a man unmindful, like Peter, of his frailty; Chrysostom looks past the moment to the disciple then weakest of all, who afterwards went over the whole earth among those who wished his death.
17:
The four days are counted before they are interpreted. Chrysostom does the arithmetic — two days stayed, the messenger a day before, and the day Lazarus died — while Henry prefers to think Lazarus died at the instant Christ said our friend sleepeth, and draws the moral that promised salvations, though they come surely, often come slowly. Alcuin says the delay was to make the raising more glorious. Augustine turns the number into four deaths: the law of our birth, the natural law transgressed, the written law despised, the Gospel transgressed — and Christ does not disdain to waken even these.

The distance is measured with unexpected care. Lightfoot notes the Jewish mile ran seven furlongs and a half, and reckons the furlong from the numeral value of its letters at two hundred and sixty-six cubits. Ellicott hears something in the past tense: this way of speaking of places is absent from the other Gospels, and may mean John wrote when the buildings no longer stood. Barnes quotes a traveller who found the reputed sepulchre a wretched cavern, every way unsatisfactory and almost disgusting.

The mourners bring their customs. Clarke and Ellicott set out the thirty days — three of weeping, seven of lamentation, twenty of sorrow — this fourth day being the first of the seven. Lightfoot describes the seven standings and sittings on the way back from the grave — partly to comfort, partly to weep, partly to meditate on mortality — though he has seen it written that they were ordained because evil spirits followed from the grave and needed that time to leave. Chrysostom asks how these Jews could console the friends of Christ, having resolved to expel his confessors, and offers sympathy, respect for the family's rank, or that these were of the better sort. Calvin turns their kindness into providence: they came to perform an office of friendship, but were assembled by a secret decree, that the miracle might not rest on the household's testimony alone — and their later blindness convicts the nation, a demonstration near the city gates, as if erected on a stage, vanishing from their eyes.

Then the sisters part ways. Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott agree that sitting was the posture of grief, sometimes so fixed as to render the mourner immovable; Robertson catches the imperfect, while Mary was sitting, finding both true to the characters Luke gave them. Chrysostom says Martha went alone to speak with Christ by herself, Theophylact because she feared the visitors would follow, Calvin and Ellicott because she could speak her heart outside the formal lamentation without exposing him. Henry reads the difference as temperament: Martha's busy nature, once a snare when she was cumbered about many things, now kept grief from her heart and carried her out first, while Mary's contemplative nature, once her advantage at his feet, left her less able to grapple with sorrow.

Her greeting is weighed by all of them. Robertson notes that Mary will use the identical words, so the sisters had said it to each other, with wistful longing if not a little reproach; Ellicott finds them tying the power to save to his bodily presence, as the courtier had. Clarke concludes they thought he could cure at hand but not at a distance, and took him for no more than a prophet; Chrysostom, that she believed, but not as she ought, nor as though he were God. Calvin is severest: her confidence rested on no promise of Christ, so she yields to her own wishes instead of submitting to him, and only a few sparks of faith shine through. Augustine hears the opposite: she does not say bring my brother to life, since she could not know whether that were good for him, but leaves it to his judgment and not her presumption. Ellicott and Wesley find in her next words a hope she dare not speak.
23:
The promise is deliberately ambiguous. Augustine points out that he does not say now, and Chrysostom that he takes a middle course, saying neither I will ask God nor I need no help, either being too much for her. Ellicott holds the words cannot exclude the bodily restoration he is about to work, yet are framed to lead her from one passionate longing toward a truer conception; Clarke reads them flatly, that is, directly. Calvin sees only kindness — he forgives her faults and offers unasked more than she had ventured to name.

Her answer is a retreat, and Ellicott makes it the chapter's most human moment: she is reminded of a general truth she had rested in before, and it does not meet the expectation she had just formed. We have all felt this beside a grave, conquering the pagan thought lost for ever and then conquered by lost for the present. Robertson asks whether that was all Jesus meant, such comfort being commonly offered and having failed her. Calvin balances her two faults: earlier she fabricated a hope out of her own feelings and went beyond her warrant, now she stops short as if alarmed when Christ stretches out his hand; we must guard against both extremes.

The answer moves the resurrection out of the calendar into a person. Ellicott dwells on the emphatic pronoun: I, and none beside me, am the Resurrection — a present life, not one lying at the remoteness of the last day, as elsewhere he is the Water and Bread of Life. Robertson takes from Westcott that resurrection is one manifestation of the Life and involved in it: not doctrines about future events but present realities. Barnes says it depends so entirely on his power and will that he may be called the resurrection itself; Clarke turns it into a question: by whom shall your brother rise, if not by me, and is it not as easy to raise him now as then? Alcuin gives the logic in a line, that he is the resurrection because he is the life; Chrysostom adds that one needing help could not be the resurrection, and being the life he is not confined by place.

Lightfoot answers the rabbis on their own ground. Let it be granted, he says, that the little bone luz in the backbone is the seed of the Jew's resurrection — Hadrian was shown a bone that water would not steep, fire not burn, the mill not grind, which cleft the anvil and broke the hammer — but ours is Jesus, who raised himself; and he wonders why they never mauled the Sadducees with the argument. Calvin takes the saying of a spiritual raising as well: faith, he says, is a resurrection of the soul, and those who talk of men being prepared for grace by the movement of nature might as well say that the dead walk. Wesley reduces it to two clauses: the resurrection of the dead, the life of the living.

The last promise is guarded carefully. Robertson marks the strong double negative and takes the death denied to be the eternal one; Ellicott says the physical fact is not denied, but through the infinite course of ages nothing shall be to the believer what the sting of death is. Calvin grounds the perpetuity on Christ's power to finish what he began, death becoming a kind of emancipation. On the confession itself they divide. Robertson ranks it above Peter's at Caesarea Philippi, since she makes hers with her brother four days buried; Ellicott finds the whole assent in the two words Yea, Lord, the rest being its ground. Chrysostom is unconvinced — she saw he meant something great without seeing what, and is asked one thing and answers another — and Clarke thinks her faith went no further, since she ran to call her sister rather than wait for more.
28:
Martha calls her sister quietly, and Augustine glosses the word: secretly means in a low voice, since she did speak. The reason is agreed by Chrysostom, Ellicott, Barnes and Calvin: the visiting Jews must not learn Christ had come, and Calvin thinks it was at Martha's request that he stayed outside the village, his late escape from stoning being fresh in her mind. The title she uses is noticed by all — not Rabbi but the Greek for teacher, which Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson take for the name he went by in that household, since Mary knows at once who is meant. Whether he had asked for her is less clear: Clarke assumes he did, to strengthen her faith beforehand, while Ellicott observes we are told only what Martha reported. Theophylact suggests his presence was itself the summons.

Mary's rising draws a small sermon from John Chrysostom. Mourning women, he says, have this malady, that they wish to be made much of on account of their case; she neither waited for the Master nor stood on what might have seemed her due. Robertson finds the same in the grammar, an ingressive aorist for the impulse and an imperfect picturing her still going. Augustine draws a quiet inference from her haste: had she known earlier, she would never have let Martha go without her.

That he had not yet entered the village is explained two ways. Chrysostom says he came on slowly so as not to seem to catch at an occasion for a miracle, but to have it pressed on him; Robertson admits we do not know. Gill and Clarke supply the topography: burial grounds lay outside the villages, so the spot was near the tomb.

The mourners follow, and the commentators divide over nuisance or providence. Robertson is blunt: this crowd meant kindly and did the one wrong thing, as people with kind notions often do, so Martha's secrecy came to nothing. Augustine and Chrysostom take the opposite view, that the Evangelist records it to show how so many came to witness the miracle, and Calvin says they were led in darkness where they never intended to go. He then turns on their kindness: it is a prevailing disease that the bereaved are eager to increase their grief by every method, and instead of dissuading her from the tomb these friends went with her — those who treat the excesses of their friends too gently do them little good by their consolations. Clarke reports the custom behind their guess: mourners visited the grave during the three days of weeping, the spirit being thought to hover about the body until it saw the face change. Lightfoot cites a rule that no man should follow a woman on the road, not even his wife, then withdraws the observation as hardly worth a grain of salt.

Mary says less than her sister, and does more. Chrysostom finds her the more fervent, forgetting the crowd and the enemies in it, thinking of nothing but giving him honour; Wesley notes Martha had not fallen at his feet, so this makes amends for her slowness. Robertson observes she used Martha's exact words and said nothing further, only wept; Ellicott guesses her emotion was too strong for speech rather than that the Jews restrained her. Bede had said as much: she could not bring out what she wanted for weeping. Calvin reads the gesture as confession, since there was nothing royal about Christ after the flesh to draw such honour, so she would not have done it unless persuaded he was the Son of God; yet in her words he finds her sister's fault, tying a power that fills heaven and earth to a bodily presence, and Theophylact calls her faith as yet imperfect. Alcuin softens it: while thou wast with us no sickness dared show itself where the Life had taken up his abode.
33:
The groaning is guarded on all sides. Augustine asks who but himself could trouble him, and answers that he was troubled because it pleased him, as he hungered because it pleased him to hunger. Theophylact says he sometimes gave that nature free vent and sometimes restrained it, to prove himself truly man and to teach the measure of grief, absence of sympathy being brutal and excess of it unmanly. Henry fastens on the idiom — he troubled himself — concluding he was never troubled but when he troubled himself, voluntary in his compassion as in his passion.

The question that follows is asked by one who knows it. Augustine says he asked to try their faith, and hears an allusion to our hidden calling, the Lord seeming ignorant while we are ignorant ourselves; Chrysostom, that he would not thrust the miracle on them but be asked for it, removing suspicion. Henry adds the practical reason: had he gone straight to the grave the Jews would have suspected a trick, and a serious address to our work is the best cure for inordinate grief. Robertson takes it as a plain request for direction, come and see being Philip's language to Nathanael, though these speakers had no notion of his purpose.

Then the shortest verse. Robertson presses the word, an ingressive aorist of a verb that never means to wail — Jesus burst into tears. Ellicott makes the same distinction, not the cry of lamentation but the calm shedding of tears, and turns it into an apology: a God in tears has provoked the smile of the stoic and the scorn of the unbeliever, yet humanity has never seen the divinity of the Son of Man more clearly than through his human tears. Clarke is indignant at the alternative, reporting on Epiphanius that certain ancients, improperly styled fathers of the Church, thought weeping a degradation and struck from Luke the place where Christ wept over Jerusalem. Augustine asks why Christ wept, if not to teach men to weep; Alcuin, that he wept in the nature by which he could not raise one whom he could raise by the other. Barnes concludes that religion neither forbids nor condemns such grief; Henry, that we never read he laughed, but more than once find him in tears.

The bystanders read the tears two ways. Ellicott recovers a tense in the first — how he used to love him — so they infer backwards from tears after death to affection during life; Robertson notes it is the sisters' own word, seen now even by the Jews. Clarke and Henry turn the exclamation forward: he dropped a tear and they said see how he loved him; he poured out his blood, and we may cry, behold how he hath loved us.

The second reading is a reproach. Ellicott identifies a different party, thinking not of raising the dead but of preventing it, whose real inference is that this failure discredits the opening of the blind man's eyes; Robertson notes they say could not rather than cannot, that miracle of three months back having left its impression, and finds them sharing the sisters' own view. Chrysostom says the enemies turn against him the works that should have proved his power, prejudging before he reaches the grave. Clarke calls the reasoning madness, answered by miracles of mercy or judgment that convert or confound; Wesley marvels that men who thought he might have prevented death never dreamed he could undo it. Calvin weighs the parties: the first think less highly of Christ than they ought, allowing him nothing beyond a man, yet speak more modestly than the second, who praise his power only to reproach him with withholding it. So men always do, complaining the moment God declines one wish — a twofold disease, subjecting him to the desires of the flesh and hurrying him before the time.
38:
He groans again, and the cause is disputed. Ellicott and Robertson trace it to the sneer just uttered, the speculation about his power stirring his nature again, and Gill calls it holy anger at their malice; Calvin thinks he contemplated the transaction rather than the men, approaching the sepulchre not as an idle spectator but as a champion preparing for a contest, the tyranny of death set before his eyes. The grave was a rock cave closed by a stone, which Robertson says kept animals off. Ellicott notes the sepulchre shown to travellers is entered from above by twenty-six steps, suiting the phrase lay upon it, though he warns the identification is doubtful — and Clarke asks how, on that arrangement, Lazarus could have come forth.

Why the stone had to be shifted by hand gets one answer. Chrysostom puts the objection first: he who moved a dead body by his voice could surely have moved a stone. He would not, so the miracle should happen in full sight and none could say, as of the blind man, that this was not the same person; now they might go in and feel and see. Robertson notes they could do that much without any exercise of divine power, and Gill that it broke a rule forbidding a grave to be opened once stopped up — but a greater than the fathers of the traditions was present. Henry draws the line exactly: men can prepare the way and take away the stone, and Christ alone gives life.

Martha's protest turns on an idiom. Robertson reports the text says only he is a fourth-day man, an ordinal Herodotus uses of one four days dead; the verb means simply to give out an odour, good or bad. Ellicott alone questions the inference: the text does not say decomposition had begun, and the assumption is opposed by the interval during which the sepulchre stood open while Jesus prayed. Lightfoot supplies the belief behind her words: for three days the spirit hovers about the tomb hoping to return, and leaves only when it sees the face changed, after which no corpse may be certified as this man and no other — though Robertson adds there is no suggestion Martha held it.

How much unbelief the protest carries divides them. Ellicott catches a nuance in the naming: not simply Martha speaks, but that in Martha which was sister to the dead man, unable to bear that any eyes should see the form she loved gone to corruption. Bede takes the words for wonder rather than despair, while Theophylact and Augustine hear weakness of faith. Calvin is harshest: she measures an incomprehensible power by the perception of her flesh, and while we stretch out one hand to ask help we repel with the other the help offered — she was first to meet him, no ordinary proof of piety, and yet throws difficulties in his way. Wesley says it in six words, that reason and faith struggled together. Origen draws the rule that nothing should come between Jesus' commands and the doing of them.

The reply quotes a promise John never recorded, as Gill, Wesley and Calvin note; Robertson takes it for the believest thou this of the earlier conversation, calling Bernard's difficulty over it far-fetched. Ellicott hears gentleness not wholly without rebuke, and insists the glory of God means more than a body restored, unbelievers having seen that too. Calvin makes faith the condition of the display: it prepares the way for that power, as in the promise to open the mouth wide that it may be filled, while unbelief keeps his hands shut, which is why he could do no mighty work at home. Cyril of Jerusalem draws out the implication, that some are saved by others' faith: what the dead man lacked his sisters supplied, and their faith recalled him from the gates of hell.
41:
The lifted eyes are posture, not rule. Calvin calls them the token of a mind prepared for prayer, yet warns that hypocrites can draw down heaven by a stern aspect while the publican with his face to the ground pierces it. Robertson infers that Jesus had prayed already and has the answer before he acts, quoting Dods: no pomp of incantation, no wrestling in prayer even, but simple thanksgiving as if Lazarus were restored. Ellicott corrects the tense to thou didst hear me and looks for the unrecorded moment of that prayer; Origen reads the gesture mystically, as the lifting of the mind by prayer, and bids us pray after that pattern. Clarke supplies a reason of the hour: since great wonders were commonly thought possible by the devil's power, he invoked the supreme God aloud, that no hindrance to faith remained.

The clause that follows is where the doctrine is fought over. Chrysostom denies that thou hast heard me confesses any lack of power, calling it the language of friends and equals, and adds that Christ hides his meaning because of his hearers' weak faith — God regarding our salvation more than his dignity, so lofty sayings are few and obscure while humble ones abound. Hilary puts it exactly: he did not need to pray but prayed for our sakes, and the prayer benefited not himself but our faith — he wanted no help, we wanted instruction. Alcuin allows that as man he is inferior and prays; Ellicott presses the emphatic pronoun, I for my part knew, and calls this union of wills the law of his human life.

The cry is deliberately loud. Robertson says it was not for Lazarus but the crowd, that they might see him come forth simultaneously with the command, and notes the Greek has no verb, only two adverbs — hither, out. Ellicott observes this is the only place the word for crying aloud is used of Christ, thinks life returned at that moment, and hears him rousing a friend by name — which Augustine says was necessary lest he bring out all the dead. Theophylact takes the voice for the trumpet of the general resurrection, loud against the Gentile fable that the soul stayed in the tomb. Chrysostom notes he says not arise but come forth, and not in my Father's name, throwing off the appearance of one praying: his words show humility, his acts power.

That a bound man walked divides them. Ellicott quotes Basil's exclamation, a wonder within a wonder, and reports that older expositors made the movement a second miracle, he declines it, since the order to loose him tells against it, the limbs being perhaps wrapped separately. Lightfoot takes the opposite view, that the Evangelist is particular about the bands and napkin to hint at a second miracle inside the great one.

The last command is read two ways. Chrysostom hears humility, since he does not take Lazarus about for display, and evidence besides, since by touching him they could be certain. Calvin makes it wholly evidential: Christ could have loosed the bands himself, but chose to employ the hands of the spectators as witnesses — and he turns on those who draw auricular confession from the words, the order having been given to the Jews and not to the disciples. Augustine and Gregory read exactly what Calvin refuses. To come forth is to leave the hiding place and condemn oneself by confession; the bands mean that those delivered from carnal things cannot be free of the flesh while in the body; the napkin, that full knowledge is not attained in this life, until in another all veils are removed and we see face to face; and loose him is spoken to the ministers, Alcuin dividing the labour: Christ wakes, his power quickening inwardly, and the disciples loose, since by the priesthood's ministry the quickened are absolved.
45:
The miracle divides its witnesses, and Henry marks the division as the usual one, a savour of life to some and of death to others: these had heard of his works and evaded them by questioning the fact, but having now seen, their unbelief was conquered. Origen weighs who the informers were — believers hoping to conciliate his opponents, or unbelievers meaning to inflame them — and decides for the second, since the Evangelist makes the believers the larger group and only some go. Henry presses further: they told no more than truth, yet malice gave their report a tincture of diabolism equal to lying, since perverting what is true is as bad as forging what is false — Doeg is called a deceitful tongue though what he said was fact.

The council that follows is described with some care. Robertson notes that chief priests and Pharisees combine in the summons, and that from this point the Sadducean priesthood takes the lead, loyally supported by its own opponents; Lazarus is nowhere named in their debate, though plainly included in the many signs. Ellicott explains the alarm — opponents have turned believers, and men of their own rank among them — so the Pharisees carry their difficulty to the chief priests. Clarke observes that Pharisees as such could not convene a council, so those meant must be scribes and elders acting with Annas and Caiaphas, the miracle being so incontestable that they were at their wit's end, their own spies having borne the testimony.

Their opening question reads as self-accusation. Robertson makes it literally what are we doing — he is active, we idle — while Ellicott hears the present tense as the confession of men who feel they have delayed too long, noting the contradiction in a sentence that grants many signs yet calls him nothing but this Man. Chrysostom says the same shortly, that they name him a man after such proofs of his divinity. Theophylact observes that a miracle which should have drawn wonder becomes the occasion of a plot; Augustine, that the wretched men considered only how to kill him, not how to be saved from death. Origen finds both audacity and blindness: audacity, that they own the miracles and still expect to prevail; blindness, that they never ask how one who did such things should fail to escape them, unless they meant to deny the power was divine.

Why they could grant the works and refuse the claim gets answers. Barnes supplies the theory that made it possible: they did not doubt an impostor might work wonders, the Egyptian magicians and the warning in Deuteronomy standing behind it. Henry says they are witnesses against themselves, acknowledging his credentials and denying his commission. Calvin puts it heavily: they assemble deliberately to bury a glory that astonishes them, setting their own industry as a shield against the divine power, as if perseverance could vanquish him. Wesley answers their question in four words — what do we? believe — adding that death yields to Christ sooner than infidelity.

The Roman plea is judged a pretext. Chrysostom asks what evidence there was of an usurper: did he take armed men about, or go with horsemen, when he chose desert places? And lest they seem to consult their own interest, they declare the whole state in danger. Henry agrees that pretended fears are the usual colour of malicious designs, the gospel being no way hurtful to kings or provinces and its teacher bidding men pay tribute to Caesar. Augustine draws the outcome: fearing to lose temporal things and never thinking of eternal life, they lost both, the Romans coming at last to take away place and nation. Lightfoot goes furthest, believing the Sanhedrin knew, or strongly suspected, whom they condemned — the vinedressers say this is the heir, and the council knew Daniel's weeks were accomplished and the Messiah's time come.
49:
The phrase high priest that same year draws attention. Clarke and Barnes explain that the office was for life under the law, but Rome and Herod raised and deposed whom they pleased; Clarke adds his proper name was Joseph, Caiaphas being a surname. Ellicott notes that Caiaphas is the Syriac form of Cephas, so he too bore the name Rockman, and hears in the thrice-repeated phrase a solemnity: that fatal and decisive year. Calvin denies the phrase means an annual office, the dignity having become purchasable and passed about contrary to a Law that meant it to end only with the holder's death.

His opening insult is scored variously. Robertson allows him the point, no solution having in fact been offered; Ellicott supposes suggestions had been made that seemed to miss the mark, and Wesley that he reproved slow deliberations in a clear case. John Chrysostom is harsher: what the others put forward doubtfully, this man cried aloud, shamelessly and audaciously.

The maxim itself is granted its plausibility and then demolished. Clarke concedes that in politics nothing could be juster, the saying being proverbial among the Jews, but answers with two words: religion forbids doing evil that good may come, and none of the premises were certain — that Christ would be acknowledged king, that he would rise against Rome, that Rome would destroy the nation. Calvin puts the argument in its true form, that they must provoke the wrath of God in order to prosper, and warns us never to separate the useful from the lawful: a people is no better protected by an innocent man's death than a body is by cutting its throat. Gill localises the pronoun: expedient for us means for the rulers, whose posts were at stake. Robertson notes the preposition will carry instead of as well as for, and observes drily that politicians are often willing to sacrifice the other fellow.

That such a man should prophesy is the difficulty. Lightfoot asks it bluntly — is Caiaphas among the prophets, when there had been none among the priests for four hundred years? — and dismisses as not worth confuting the notion that the office conferred the gift. The Evangelist, he says, points at the year and not the man: it was the year of an outpouring beyond anything the world had seen, and some drops might fall on a wicked man as crumbs fall to the dog beneath the table, so that witness to the redemption came from the Redeemer's greatest enemy — and by just reckoning the high priesthood itself expired that year. Origen separates act from character: not everyone who prophesies is a prophet, and Caiaphas prophesied as Balaam did. Chrysostom says divine grace used his mouth but never touched his corrupt heart; Calvin gives him two tongues, one vomiting his own design while God turned the other to a prediction. Barnes cautions that prophecy here is not used strictly.

Clarke reaches for a pagan parallel, the line Virgil gives Neptune — one life shall fall that many may be saved — introduced, he thinks, in an episode neither historical nor ornamental, purely to state the poet's creed on the doctrine. Augustine reads the Evangelist's enlargement as a correction: Caiaphas meant that nation only, in which were the sheep of the house of Israel, but there were other sheep not of this fold — children of God who as yet were neither sheep nor children. Henry makes the dying both attraction and centre, gathering those far from Christ and uniting those far from each other. Gregory observes that the persecutors killed him to extinguish his followers' devotion, and faith grew from the very thing they thought would destroy it. Origen asks whether the resolve that followed came from the same Spirit as the prophecy, and answers that it need not, since men turn even the Scriptures to the support of bad doctrine.
54:
The withdrawal is defended before it is located. Augustine insists his power had not failed — he could have walked openly still — but he meant to show by example that believers do not sin in retiring out of their persecutors' sight; it is praiseworthy when the struggle comes not to avoid confession, and no less praiseworthy to avoid giving occasion for the trial, since whoever causes another's sin is answerable for it. He took the disciples along to remove the same occasion. Robertson adds that walking openly now would have brought on an end appointed for the passover a month off. Chrysostom looks at the disciples: it must have troubled them to see him save himself by merely human means, hidden and in danger while the nation kept the feast, and yet they continued with him.

Where Ephraim stood no one can say. Ellicott sets out the difficulty — the manuscripts spell it four ways, and Eusebius and Jerome both identified it with Ephron but placed it eight and twenty miles from Jerusalem — concluding that we must leave the matter in uncertainty. Clarke puts it near Bethel, where Christ stayed two months. Calvin declines the search: either the name was pronounced corruptly then or was wholly new, language and landscape both having changed greatly after the captivity. He adds that his disciples here means not all who received his doctrine but the constant companions who lived under one roof.

Origen alone reads the retreat as figure. The Word walked openly among that people while it came by the prophets; when it ceased, Jesus went thence — into the country, which is the whole world, near the wilderness, which is the deserted Church, to Ephraim, whose name means fruitfulness. Ephraim was the younger brother of Manasseh, whose name means forgotten: when the elder people were passed over there came an abundant harvest from the Gentiles, and there he continues with his disciples to this day.

The purifications draw out the antiquarians, then a correction. Lightfoot reports the rule that every man is bound to purify himself for the feast, and the graduated times — a whole week for one defiled by a dead body, sprinkled on the third day and the seventh with water mixed from the ashes of the red heifer — while shaving and washing garments counted too. But Ellicott points out that the Law ordained no special purification before the passover, only the general requirement of cleanness, and Calvin makes the same point from the text: the Evangelist writes many and not all, the sanctification being voluntary. Augustine sets the two feasts against each other: they meant to keep that passover by shedding the very blood which consecrates it, and where theirs was kept in the dark with doorposts stained by a slain animal, ours is kept in the light with the sign on the forehead.

The last verses are a manhunt. Robertson notes they had sought him at tabernacles six months before but now mean to kill him, and finds in the perfect participle the knots of people standing about the temple precincts, their question framed to assume he will not dare come. Ellicott hears continued seeking and speaking, day after day, and two questions rather than one. Barnes turns it to use: danger stood on one side and duty on the other, and he chose duty, leaving the event with God. Origen observes that the Evangelist calls it the Jews' passover and not the Lord's, since it was then they plotted his death, and that the warrant confesses they did not know where he was. Theophylact adds that had the people alone done this the Passion might have been laid to ignorance, but the Pharisees give the order; and Alcuin turns the search around: they sought him with bad intent, while we seek him in God's temple, praying him to come to our feast.
